newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police step aside for angry protesters.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police step aside for angry protesters.

text.p: Albanian police stepped aside on Saturday and let thousands of cheated investors march to demand that the government reimburse millions of dollars in losses and then quit.

"Down with the government", "Police are with us", chanted about 1,000 people in Fier, 110 km (70 miles) south of Tirana. Earlier several thousand people marched through the port town of Vlore, further south, for an 11th day.
No riot police could be seen as the protesters marched from Fier's town centre to the prefecture, shouting slogans and waving to television cameras.
A senior police commander, who declined to be named, said: "There is no problem. We have withdrawn the riot police. Let them demonstrate. It's their right."

Many people trailed the procession along main streets, some fearing a repeat of attacks by civilians armed with clubs and iron bars earlier this week in Fier. Six people were injured in the attack, one seriously.
When the noisy crowd walked past the street leading to the police station before it turned back to the square, they jeered at up to 40 uniformed policemen guarding the passage to their station.

About 70 to 80 riot policemen could be seen behind them in full gear and four policemen with submachine-guns mounted guard on the roof of the police station. But no police tried to block the marchers' route as had happened in recent days.

Earlier in Vlore, about 4,000 people marched to the prefecture, carrying the picture of another demonstrator, Maliq Banushi, 51, who died of a heart attack during protests this week. "Police killed him" was written below his photograph.

One demonstrator was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks in Vlore earlier this week. About 150 people were injured in Albania's worst unrest since 40 years of communist rule collapsed in 1990.
Traffic police accompanied the crowd Vlore. Police had fled the town after the clashes on Monday and returned only a few days later.
Police commanders said traffic police are back on duty and about 80 percent of the regular police force is also working again.

Demonstrators had stoned, stripped and then expelled the Vlore police during Monday's violence, plunging the 90,000 residents of Albania's second port into scenes of lawlessness, crime and smuggling of would-be-refugees to Italy.
Vlore has been the scene of some of the worst violence since the high-risk pyramid investment schemes began collapsing in January.
Many people in the town have been financially ruined since Vlore's local Gjallica scheme collapsed, and they accuse the right-wing government of letting the schemes flourish over the past five years.
Officials in Tirana said that prosecutors have now issued international arrest warrants for the failed Gjallica scheme's president Shemsie Kadria and her husband, Gani.

Reports vary widely on how much money was lost by the five companies which have now gone bust. News reports in Tirana said Kadria and her husband fled to Turkey and owed creditors $363 million. Other reporters have put the figure at $500 million.
Gjallica's businesses and the personal assets of managers have been seized. The government has ordered banks and other high-interest schemes to freeze deposits of Gjallica managers.
A Tirana appeals court upheld jail sentences of up to three years for three managers of the Arkond firm and ordered them each to pay $150,000 to investors in the scheme which collapsed last year.
Protests by angry investors were expected in numerous towns on Saturday, including Vlore, Fier and Tepelene in the south, and Mirdite in the north.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been swept by riots and protests over the past month after thousands of investors lost their savings in the failed schemes.
The schemes lured new money with offers of high interest rates and then used the cash to pay earlier investors. A large proportion of Albania's adults seem to have joined the schemes.
The companies often built holiday resorts, petrol stations, motels, supermarket chains and other high-profile investments, giving the illusion of success.
Their offices were often guarded by police and ministers joined in ground-breaking ceremonies, giving the impression that the schemes were sanctioned by the government.
That led investors to turn their wrath on President Sali Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, blaming them for letting the dubious schemes evolve.
